passage: dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely
text:
The passage says the Transformer removes recurrence and convolutions completely and relies only on attention. The image shows the abstract line "mechanism. We propose a new simple network architecture, the Transformer, based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely." p. 1

Recurrence means processing a sequence one step at a time, where each step depends on the previous hidden state, as in recurrent neural networks. Convolutions are operations that slide a small window across the input to combine nearby items. Dropping both means the model does not rely on either mechanism to handle word order or context.

Here, this is the central claim: attention alone, which lets every position relate directly to every other position, replaces the sequential and windowed machinery. The document explains that this allows more parallel computation during training. p. 2

passage: This inherently sequential nature precludes parallelization within training examples
text:
The sentence says that because recurrent models must process one step after another, their training cannot be spread across parallel computation within a single training example.

The passage explains that a recurrent model computes each hidden state h_t from the previous hidden state h_(t-1) and the input at position t. Each step therefore has to wait for the one before it. "Precludes parallelization within training examples" means this waiting rules out doing the steps for one example at the same time. p. 2

This matters most for long sequences, because memory limits how many examples can be batched together, so the only remaining speed-up is inside each example. p. 2

Here the point sets up the paper's motivation: the Transformer is proposed to avoid this sequential chain, which is why it can be more parallelizable. p. 1

question: Why would large dot products push the softmax into regions with tiny gradients?
text:
The document gives the setup but not the full explanation, so the second half here is from general knowledge.

What the paper says: footnote 4 assumes the components of q and k are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1. Then the dot product has mean 0 and variance dk p. 4. So as dk grows, the typical size of the dot products grows too (standard deviation of √dk), which is why the authors divide by √dk.

Why that hurts the softmax (general knowledge): softmax exponentiates its inputs, so when one score is much larger than the others, nearly all the weight goes to that one entry. The output becomes close to a one-hot vector, a saturated region. There, the softmax's derivative is the weight times (1 minus the weight), or products of weights, and these approach zero when weights are near 0 or 1. Small changes to the inputs barely change the output, so gradients passed back are tiny and learning stalls. Scaling by 1/√dk brings the variance of the scores back to about 1, keeping the softmax in a more responsive range.

question: Why use 8 smaller heads instead of one big attention head?
text:
The paper gives two reasons. The first is in the sentence you selected: multi-head attention lets the model jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions, whereas with a single head, averaging inhibits this p. 5. A single softmax-weighted sum blends everything into one averaged vector, so one head can't easily focus on several kinds of relationships at once. The background section makes a related point, saying the averaging of attention-weighted positions reduces effective resolution, and that multi-head attention counteracts this p. 2.

The second reason is cost. Each head uses dk = dv = dmodel/h = 64, so the total computational cost is similar to single-head attention at full dimensionality p. 5.

The ablation supports this. Holding computation constant, a single head was 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting, though quality also dropped with too many heads (32 heads scored 25.4 against 25.8 for 8 and 16) p. 9.

The paper doesn't explain why the quality falls off at high head counts. From general knowledge, a plausible cause is that each head's key dimension becomes too small, which fits their finding that reducing dk hurts quality.

A single softmax-weighted sum blends everything into one averaged vector, so one head can't easily focus on several kinds of relationships at once. The background section makes a related point, saying the averaging of attention-weighted positions reduces effective resolution, and that multi-head attention counteracts this p. 2.

The second reason is cost. Each head uses dk = dv = dmodel/h = 64, so the total computational cost is similar to single-head attention at full dimensionality p. 5.

The ablation supports this. Holding computation constant, a single head was 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting, though quality also dropped with too many heads (32 heads scored 25.4 against 25.8 for 8 and 16) p. 9.

The paper doesn't explain why the quality falls off at high head counts. From general knowledge, a plausible cause is that each head's key dimension becomes too small, which fits their finding that reducing dk hurts quality.

question: What is label smoothing, and why would it help BLEU while hurting perplexity?
text:
The document only names the technique and states its effect; it doesn't define label smoothing or explain the mechanism. It says the authors used a value of ε_ls = 0.1, citing Szegedy et al. [36], and that it "hurts perplexity, as the model learns to be more unsure, but improves accuracy and BLEU score" p. 8.

From general knowledge: label smoothing changes the training target. Instead of asking the model to put probability 1 on the correct token and 0 on every other, you take a small share (here 0.1) and spread it across the other tokens. The model is therefore penalized for being fully confident.

That explains the trade-off. Perplexity measures how much probability the model assigns to the exact reference tokens, so a model deliberately held back from high confidence scores worse on it. BLEU only checks whether the output translation matches the reference, and the usual explanation is that avoiding overconfidence helps the model generalize and rank candidates better during beam search. The document itself doesn't give that second part, only the observed result.

passage: We also experimented with using learned positional embeddings
question: If learned embeddings performed the same, why keep the sinusoids?
text:
The document gives one reason: the sinusoidal version "may allow the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than the ones encountered during training." p. 6 A learned embedding table only has entries for positions seen in training, so it has nothing to offer beyond that length, while a sinusoid can be computed for any position.

There is a second, related motivation earlier on the same page. The authors hypothesized that sinusoids would make it easy to attend by relative position, because for any fixed offset k, PE(pos+k) can be written as a linear function of PE(pos). p. 6

Note that the document only states this extrapolation benefit as a possibility ("may"). It does not test it, since the comparison in Table 3 row (E) is on the same English-to-German development set, where the two versions score 25.7 versus 25.8 BLEU. p. 9 So the choice rests on a plausible advantage rather than a measured one.

passage: beam search with a beam size of
question: What does a beam size of 4 mean in practice?
text:
The document doesn't explain beam search itself; it only says the models used a beam size of 4 with length penalty α = 0.6, chosen after experimentation on the development set p. 8. What follows is from general knowledge.

When the decoder generates a translation one token at a time, the simplest approach (greedy decoding) keeps only the single most probable next token at each step. Beam search instead keeps the 4 best partial translations at every step. Each of those 4 candidates is extended by every possible next token, the resulting sequences are scored by their cumulative log-probability, and only the top 4 survive to the next step. This continues until candidates finish, and the best-scoring finished sequence is returned.

A larger beam explores more alternatives and can find higher-probability outputs, at the cost of more computation. A beam of 1 is the same as greedy decoding. The length penalty matters because summed log-probabilities favor short outputs, so the score is adjusted to avoid that bias.

For comparison, the parsing experiments used a larger beam of 21 p. 10.

question: What limitations of the Transformer do the authors themselves acknowledge?
text:
The authors never give the limitations their own section, so these are admissions scattered through the document and the work they list as future.

Reduced resolution: relating any two positions in a constant number of operations comes "at the cost of reduced effective resolution due to averaging attention-weighted positions," which multi-head attention is meant to counteract p. 2.

Long sequences: self-attention is faster than recurrence only when the sequence length n is smaller than the representation dimension d p. 6. For very long inputs they suggest restricting attention to a neighborhood of size r, which raises the maximum path length to O(n/r), and they leave this for future work p. 7.

The compatibility function: shrinking dk hurts quality, which they take to suggest that a more sophisticated function than dot product may be beneficial p. 9. Too many heads also hurts p. 9.

Sequential generation: the decoder is auto-regressive, producing one element at a time p. 2, and the conclusion names "making generation less sequential" as a goal p. 10.

Scope: handling images, audio and video is a plan, not a result p. 10. On parsing, the model beat every earlier reported model except the Recurrent Neural Network Grammar p. 10.

question: How does the base model differ from the big model, and what did each cost to train?
text:
Size, training length and dropout differ between the two.

Base model: 6 layers, dmodel = 512, dff = 2048, 8 heads with dk = dv = 64, dropout 0.1, and 65M parameters p. 9. It trained for 100,000 steps at about 0.4 seconds per step, roughly 12 hours on 8 P100 GPUs p. 7.

Big model: 6 layers, dmodel = 1024, dff = 4096, 16 heads, dropout 0.3, and 213M parameters p. 9. It trained for 300,000 steps at about 1.0 second per step, which is 3.5 days on the same 8 GPUs p. 7. For English-to-French, the big model used dropout 0.1 instead of 0.3 p. 8.

Cost in FLOPs: Table 2 lists 3.3 · 10 for the base model and 2.3 · 10 for the big model, but the exponents are not legible in the printed table p. 8. The paper's method is training time × number of GPUs × sustained per-GPU capacity, using 9.5 TFLOPS for a P100 p. 8. Applying that gives about 3.3 · 10^18 for base and 2.3 · 10^19 for big, so the big model costs roughly 7 times more compute. That is my calculation, not a printed figure.

Quality: English-to-German BLEU is 27.3 for base and 28.4 for big, and English-to-French is 38.1 and 41.8 p. 8. Section 6.1 gives the big model's French score as 41.0, which conflicts with the 41.8 in the abstract and table, and the document does not explain the discrepancy p. 8.

question: Which ablation results in Table 3 matter most, and why?
text:
Table 3 is on page 9, and the printed table shows which values changed in each row, so I can be more specific than before.

Row (A), heads: with computation held roughly constant, one head (dk = 512) gets 24.9 BLEU, 4 heads 25.5, 8 heads (base) 25.8, 16 heads 25.8, and 32 heads 25.4 p. 9. The paper notes single-head attention is 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting and that too many heads also hurts p. 9. This is the core support for multi-head attention.

Row (B), dk reduced to 16 or 32: BLEU falls to 25.1 and 25.4. The authors conclude that compatibility is not easy to determine and that a more sophisticated function than dot product may help p. 9.

Row (C), size: 2 layers gives 23.7 BLEU, while dmodel = 1024 gives 26.0 and dff = 4096 gives 26.2. Bigger is better p. 9.

Row (D), regularization: no dropout drops BLEU to 24.6, so dropout matters for over-fitting p. 9. Label smoothing at 0.0 gives 25.3 and at 0.2 gives 25.7; the paper does not comment on this beyond the training description p. 8.

Row (E): learned positional embeddings give 25.7 against 25.8, so the choice barely matters p. 9.

Before you start
×

The paper proposes the Transformer, a translation architecture built only on attention, with no recurrence or convolution. It matters because it aims for better quality and far faster parallel training, and the rest of the paper describes, motivates and tests that design.

Key claims

1
The Transformer relies entirely on attention to draw global dependencies between input and output, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions. p. 2
2
Self-attention relates any two positions in a constant number of sequential operations, versus O(n) for recurrent layers. p. 6
3
The big model reaches 28.4 BLEU on WMT 2014 English-to-German, beating prior results including ensembles by over 2 BLEU. p. 8
4
Ablations show single-head attention is 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting, and quality also drops with too many heads. p. 9
5
A 4-layer Transformer with little task-specific tuning performs well on English constituency parsing, including with only 40K WSJ training sentences. p. 10

Keep in mind

The English-to-French big model score appears as 41.8 in the abstract and Table 2 but as 41.0 in the text of section 6.1. Check which figure you rely on.
Attention itself is not new. The novelty claimed is using it without recurrent or convolutional layers, so read the Background section with that distinction in mind.
Perplexities in Table 3 are per-wordpiece under byte-pair encoding, so they should not be compared with per-word perplexities from other work. Training cost figures are estimates built from GPU time and assumed sustained TFLOPS.
